fullText: Seen from the sky, this country is a sea of its own. Deep green pine forest rolling on for hours, broken only by the silver flash of a 100,000 lakes. Off its coast, a quarter of a million islands lie scattered across the Baltic like stars poured out on dark water. And in the far north, past the Arctic [music] Circle, the trees thin out into snow fields where for part of every year, the sun does not rise at all. This is Sweden, a quiet kingdom of 10 and a half million people, stretched 1,600 km from the beachwoods [music] of the south to the reindeer plains of the north. Home to more islands than any other country on Earth. [music] Here is the strange part. These people hand over some of Europe's heaviest taxes and almost none of them [music] want to live anywhere else. They treat silence not as something missing but as something earned. And right now above the Arctic Circle, an entire city is quietly packing up. Houses, clock tower, church and all, and moving 3 km across the [music] tundra before the ground beneath it gives way. [music] Today we cross Sweden from school children pedalling through falling snow to a 672 ton [music] church rolling down a road chasing one question. What kind of country rather than lose a single town would choose to pick it up and carry it? Stay with us all the way to the end. You will watch that church take its walk half a kilometer an hour with a king in the crowd. Morning in Sweden [music] starts earlier than the sun. In the blue half light of winter, [music] small figures glide along the bike paths. Children, some no older than seven, pedalling themselves to school through falling snow. Reflective vests glow over their snowsuits. No parent hovers behind them. Here, a child finding their own way through a dark morning is not [music] neglect. It is the first lesson in a lifelong course called managing on your own. The country around them runs like [music] a well-kept clock. Trains arrive when the timet says they will and people apologize when they are 3 minutes late. At the bus stop, strangers stand a full arms length apart, sometimes two, in a neat, unspoken line that no one organized and no one breaks, [music] nobody honks, nobody pushes. The morning simply proceeds, calm and [music] exact, as if the whole nation had rehearsed it the night before. [music] To see how deep the order goes, step into the basement of any apartment building and find the Tetuga, the communal laundry room. There is a booking board and your reserved hours are close to sacred. Finish on time, wipe the machines, and above all, [music] clean the lint filter. Forgetting it is not a crime in any court, but neighbors will remember it [music] longer than they would a scandal. one small room and inside it the entire Swedish social [music] contract. The same evenness runs upward through society since a quiet language reform in the 1960s. Almost everyone here is addressed by their first name. the bus driver, the professor, the chief executive of the company. A junior employee can question the boss across the table and the boss is expected to listen. Titles exist on paper. In the room, there are just people speaking calmly one at [music] a time. None of this is enforced [music] by cameras or fines. It rests on a single assumption made 10 million times a day that the other person will do their part. Swedes [music] have a word for this deep social trust till it and it is spelled the same forward and backward which feels almost too fitting. It is the invisible machinery [music] of the country. And as you will see, it can carry far heavier things than a laundry schedule. [music] At around 10:00 in the morning and again at [music] 3:00, something remarkable happens in offices across Sweden. Work stops, not secretly, not guilty, officially. Colleagues rise from their desks, gather around coffee and a plate of cinnamon buns and talk about anything except the project due on Friday. This is Fica and no meeting, no deadline and no visiting executive is important enough to cancel it. Fica is usually translated as a coffee break [music] and every Swede will tell you the translation fails. It works as a verb just as well as a noun. Euphica with someone on purpose. The coffee matters. Swedes drink [music] more of it than almost anyone on the planet. The canalbula soft and smelling of cardamom and cinnamon matters too. But the real point is the pause itself. A small shared agreement that human beings are not machines. [music] When the clock reaches 5, the office is empty. And this is not slacking. It is the system working. A standard week is 40 hours. And staying late is quietly read not as devotion, but as a planning problem. Results count. Hours do not. By 5, the man who ran the morning [music] meeting is in the supermarket with a shopping list. And by 6, he is picking up his daughter, and no one finds this remarkable. [music] [music] Walk into a cafe on a Tuesday afternoon and you meet the most photographed proof of it. A table of men in their 30s, each with a stroller parked beside him and a sleeping baby inside. Swedes [music] call them latte dads with a smile. Behind them stands one of the most generous parental [music] systems anywhere. 480 paid days for every child split between the parents with three months reserved for each so that neither can quietly hand their share [music] away. Ask a Swede what all this wealth is for. The salaries, the technology, the taxes. And the answer once you translate it out of politeness is usually the same time. Time to eat dinner as a family at 6. Time to vanish to the forest in July. Time to sit for 15 minutes in the afternoon with coffee and a warm bun and someone worth talking to. In [music] Sweden, that is not the reward for a successful life. That is the definition of one. [music] Drive south into Smoland and the land tells you honestly how hard it once was. Granite boulders the size of cars [music] lie scattered through the forest, dropped by the ice age and never moved. The soil between them is thin and stubborn. For centuries, families here cleared [music] stones by hand, spring after spring, and learned a character to match the ground. Repair [music] what breaks, waste nothing, expect little, endure. It is no accident that [music] IKEA, an empire of plain and affordable things. [music] began in exactly this province. In the 1800s, the stones won. Harvests failed, farms [music] could not be divided any further, and the poorest corners of Sweden began to [music] empty. Between roughly 1850 and 1930, about 1.3 million Swedes from a nation of only a few million packed trunks, walked to the harbors, and boarded ships [music] for America. Whole parishes lost half their young people. Pastors [music] read farewell blessings on the docks for passengers they knew they would never see again. [music] Most of them went where the landscape looked like home. Minnesota lakes, birch trees, hard winters [music] became the most Swedish place outside Sweden itself. By 1910, more than one person in [music] 10 there was of Swedish stock. Today, over 3 million Americans still claim Swedish roots. [music] If your great grandmother left a stony farm in Smoland with a Bible and one good coat, this quiet [music] green province is where her story and part of yours began. The ones who stayed built the country the immigrants never got [music] to see. And they built it on an almost reckless level of trust. [music] On summer roads, you still pass small unmanned farm stands. [music] Strawberries, eggs, new potatoes, a price list, and an open [music] cash box. You pick what you want, drop your payment into the box, and drive on. Nobody [music] watches. The box is always right or close enough that no one has bothered to change the system in a 100red years. [music] Within two generations, one of Europe's [music] poorest countries became one of its most comfortable. But the character formed between the [music] stones never really left. Swedes still repair before they replace. Still distrust [music] flash, still praise a thing by calling it practical. They even have a word that polices [music] it all. Lagom. Neither too much nor too little, but exactly right. Keep that word with you. By the end of this journey, [music] you will see how far a country can carry it. [music] Now look [music] at the map again because Sweden saves its most absurd number for the sea. 267,570 islands, more than any other country on Earth. Most have no name you would recognize and no inhabitants at all. They are granite backs rising from the Baltic, wearing a few pines visited by gulls and the occasional kayak. No nation on the planet owns more islands and no nation thinks about it less. [music] The capital itself is an archipelago wearing a city. Stockholm [music] stands on 14 islands stitched together by more than [music] 50 bridges where the fresh water of Lake Malaren finally meets the salt of the Baltic. Commuters here take feries [music] the way others take the bus, reading their phones as the hull cuts through water that glitters all the way to the palace. 10 minutes from Parliament, there are islands with more herands than people. [music] When summer comes, the city quietly reverses itself. Families lock their apartments and migrate out into the Stockholm Archipelago, a swarm of nearly 30,000 islands to small wooden cottages [music] painted the same deep fall red their greatgrandparents used. At the stuga, life [music] shrinks to a dock, a rowboat, a swim before breakfast, and berries picked in a tin cup. The wealthiest man on the island is impossible to [music] identify, which is exactly how everyone wants it. [music] Far out in the Baltic waits the [music] strangest island of them all, Gotland, and its walled town of Visby, where a ring of [music] 13th century stone still circles the streets almost unbroken. [music] Seven centuries ago, this was one of the mightiest trading towns of the northern seas. Then history [music] moved on and simply forgot to demolish it. Roses climb the ruins of Gothic churches. Along the coast, limestone [music] stacks called Raar stand in the shallows like statues no one remembers carving. [music] Evening on a Baltic island is its own slow ceremony. The water flattens to glass. The light turns to honey and refuses [music] to leave. And the only sounds are rigging tapping on masts and someone [music] somewhere laughing at a dinner table outdoors. Sweden has grand sights as we will see. But ask a Swede [music] to close their eyes and picture happiness and odds are they will picture this. An island, a red cottage, and nothing on [music] the calendar at all. Cross now to the opposite coast where the sea air turns sharp with salt and [music] the granite shore lies bare and smooth as bone. Here wedged into [music] the rocks sits smoggan. A fishing village that looks handpainted. Boat houses in red, mustard, rust, and [music] blue stand shoulderto-shoulder on stilts above the water, joined by a long wooden boardwalk that [music] caks pleasantly underfoot. It has been photographed at [music] times and somehow still feels like a secret. [music] For generations, everything here came from the sea and [music] went back to it. Boats slipped out before dawn for herring, mackerel, and lang, and the catch was sorted [music] on the same planks tourists now stroll in summer sandals. The old fish auction has quieted, but the rhythm survives. Shrimp [music] sandwiches piled improbably high. Boats unloading in the morning. And old men on [music] benches who can read tomorrow's weather in tonight's horizon. [music] And then there is the can sewer strumming. Baltic herring salted and fermented until it becomes by most [music] accounts the strongest smelling food in the world. Swedes open it outdoors, never indoors, [music] preferably downwind in late August. Foreign visitors [music] film themselves trying it and gagging. But watch a northern family [music] at a proper sir strumming table. Flatbread, potatoes, onions, butter, and you see something else entirely. Not a dare, a memory. It tastes, they will tell you. like late summer at grandmother's. In the evening, the village exhales. [music] Gulls settle on the roof ridges. Nets and boys hang along [music] walls like decorations that never meant to be decorative. The water between the boatouses turns pink, then put somewhere. A screen door bangs. A radio murmurs a weather report and the boardwalk empties until its lamps are just a [music] string of soft lights between the rocks and the sea. [music] There is no monument in Smogen and nothing to achieve. That is rather the point. The Swedish coast does not ask to be conquered. It asks to be sat [music] beside quietly, preferably with coffee. Places like this are where the country practices its oldest skill, doing less [music] slowly near water before the seasons turn and ask everything of it. If you want to see Swedes abandon their famous [music] restraint, come on the Friday closest to the longest day of the year. Midsummer is the true national holiday, whatever the calendar claims. [music] In meadows across the country, a birch leafed pole is raised [music] and around it dance three generations wearing crowns of wild flowers. [music] Grandmothers, teenagers, toddlers, all singing the same songs about small frogs. Songs everyone pretends to find silly and no one will ever give up. [music] [music] The table is as fixed as scripture. Herring pickled a dozen [music] ways. The summer's first potatoes with dill and butter, sour cream and chives, then strawberries [music] under cream. Brighter for having ripened so slowly in the long light. There are small glasses of snaps [music] and songs required before drinking them. By law of tradition, at least one uncle will sing too [music] loudly. By morning, the meadow is quiet and the flower crowns are wilting on kitchen [music] tables saved anyway. [music] And through all of it, the sun refuses to leave. South of the mountains, it dips below the horizon for barely a few hours. North of the Arctic Circle, it does not set [music] at all from late May until the middle of July. Midnight [music] looks like late afternoon. Birds get confused and sing at 2:00 in the morning. Children are sent to bed in broad daylight [music] and accept it with the weariness of people who have lost this argument every June of their lives. [music] Summer is also when the forest opens its accounts. An old right called Alamance, [music] the freedom to roam, lets anyone walk, camp and night, swim, [music] and pick berries and mushrooms on almost any land owned by anyone [music] so long as nothing is disturbed and nothing destroyed. Families disappear among the pines with buckets and return with blueberries, linggon berries, and chanterels the color of egg yolk. The forest belongs to everyone here the way the sea belongs [music] to no one. [music] In August, the light begins its retreat, and Sweden throws it one last party. The Craftska, the crayfish feast, fills gardens with paper lanterns [music] shaped like grinning moons, ridiculous paper hats, and mountains of bright [music] red crayfish boiled with crown dill. The songs are louder now and slightly wistful. Everyone at the table knows what the shortening evenings are quietly announcing, [music] and nobody says it out loud. [music] It comes on slowly, then all at once. By November, the afternoon [music] sun is gone before the school's empty. And by December, in the far north, it barely arrives at all. This is the hour when Sweden performs its [music] oldest trick. Walk any street at dusk and look up at the windows. Paper stars, glowing amber, sevenarmed candle lamps, small, warm constellations switched on against the blue [music] dark. No one ordered this. Every household simply answers the darkness the same way with light in small amounts everywhere. [music] [music] Friday evenings get their own ritual with a name that sounds like a hug. Freda's m Friday coziness. [music] The family gathers in wool socks in front of the television. There are blankets, candles, [music] crisps in a bowl, and by delightful national consensus, tacos. Sweden [music] has adopted Friday tacos so completely that supermarkets give the ritual its own aisle. It is not Mexican exactly. It is Swedish now, the taste of a [music] week ending softly outside [music] the cafe windows. Meanwhile, stands a sight that startles every visitor. A line of pram standing out [music] in the snow, each holding a baby, fast asleep at 10° below freezing. The parents are inside, watching through the glass, unbothered. Generations of Swedish families swear by it, that cold, clean air makes children sleep deeper and grow hardier. Whatever the science eventually rules, [music] an entire nation of rosy cheicked nappers argues their case. [music] Then on the 13th of December, in the darkest [music] week, the light gets a face. Lucia. Before dawn [music] in churches, schools and workplaces, a young woman enters in a white gown, a crown of burning candles in her hair, leading a procession of white robed [music] singers. The songs are slow and strangely sorrowful for a festival. Saffron buns are passed around. Golden as the sun, everyone is missing. Even people who believe in nothing stand very still for Luchia. This is the Swedish answer to winter and it is worth pausing [music] on. No defiance, no complaint, no pretending the dark away. Just candles, [music] saffron, wool, tacos, and each other. A hundred small warmths [music] arranged against one enormous cold. They do not try to defeat the darkness. They [music] furnish it. [music] [music] Go far enough [music] north now and the sun stops rising altogether. In Kiruna, above the Arctic Circle, it stays below the horizon for about 4 weeks [music] around the turn of the year. Noon is a long blue dusk. The snow itself seems to give off [music] the only light there is. And Swedes will tell you honestly what visitors sometimes romanticize. [music] It is hard. People are tired. Mornings blur into afternoons. The body keeps [music] asking a reasonable question. Where is the sun? And for a month there is no answer. [music] They meet it with practical [music] weapons. First alarm clocks that glow like a slow sunrise. Light therapy [music] lamps at the breakfast table bright as a June morning stared into [music] over coffee. Vitamin D on the shelf of every pharmacy. Employers [music] know the season. Schools push children outside into whatever pale daylight exists because even an hour of gray sky is medicine. It is a country running its [music] own light rations carefully all winter long. [music] But the oldest remedy is the [music] strangest one. All across Sweden, in the darkest months, people cut holes [music] in frozen lakes, heat themselves in a sauna until they glow, and then walk out and lower themselves [music] into black ice rimmed water. The body screams to refuse. They breathe slowly, [music] stay half a minute, and climb out steaming. And they describe what follows like a switch being thrown. The fog gone, the blood loud, every nerve reporting for duty. [music] Ask why they do it and the answers vary. Ask when they will stop and they laugh. Beneath the ice baths and the lamps lies something quieter, a truce [music] with winter itself. Swedes do not treat the dark season as an [music] enemy to defeat, but as a tide to move with. Sleep a little more, expect a little less. Keep the [music] candles lit and let the year breathe out. Nature slows down to survive, they will point out, and human beings are still nature. From the outside, that patience [music] looks almost like a superpower. [music] And then one day in early January, it happens in Kiruna. The date is almost an appointment around [music] the 4th. When the sun clears the tree line for the first time in a month, for just a few minutes, people step out [music] of shops. Strangers stand together in the snow. Faces turned to the same low red light, saying nothing much at all. [music] It is only the sun. It rose that morning over half the planet unremarked. But here for these few minutes, it feels like a promise being kept. [music] This is Sapmi, the land of the Sami, [music] the indigenous people of Europe's far north, whose story here is older than the country's borders [music] and older than its name. For countless generations, Sammy families have followed the [music] reindeer up to the bare mountains in summer, down into the shelter of the forests [music] in winter. The herd sets the calendar. The herd, the old saying [music] goes, decides people merely keep up. [music] Near Kiruna, a herder named Nila Ingga works the same ranges [music] his ancestors did with the Levers community west of the city. The tools have changed. snowmobiles, [music] GPS collars, weather apps, but the craft has [music] not. It is reading snow with your hands, knowing when [music] ice will hold a thousand animals, hearing sickness in a herd before you can see it. It is knowledge no university grants passed from parent [music] to child on the winter ranges and it shares this land patiently [music] with the iron that lies beneath it. The north feeds its people differently. Reindeer meat smoked or dried or simmered into stews that hold a person upright at 30 below. Fish pulled through hand cut holes [music] in lake ice. And in the marshes of late July, cloudber berries, soft amber, tart sweet, so prized that families guard their picking spots [music] like inheritances. A jar of cloudberry jam in February is not food exactly. It is stored [music] summer, opened when it is needed most. [music] And each winter on the Tory River by the village of Yukashervi, this land builds the world's least permanent landmark. Since 1989, [music] artists have cut two-tonon blocks from the frozen river and raised a hotel made of ice, halls, [music] beds, chandeliers, an entire glowing palace, knowing precisely what [music] spring will do to it. Guests sleep on reindeer hides at minus 5 and call it unforgettable. In May, the whole thing melts and slides quietly back into the river it came from, leaving nothing behind. They rebuild it anyway, [music] every single year, differently. And no one involved finds this futile. It may be the most Swedish building on earth precisely because it vanishes. Beauty in the exact size of a season. Ambition melted back down to Lam by April. The far north keeps teaching one lesson in a 100 forms. Nothing here is owned. Everything is borrowed from the river, from the winter, from the land. Which brings us finally to the town that learned that lesson the hardest way of all. [music] Karuna exists because of what lies under it. The largest underground iron or mine in the world. For more than a century, this town of wooden houses above the Arctic Circle [music] has lived on iron. The mine built the church, the railway, the hospital. The very idea of a city this far north. Its main working level now lies 1,365 [music] m down. And from that depth comes a shadow. The ground above [music] the or body is slowly, irreversibly cracking. [music] So in 2004, Sweden made a decision that still sounds [music] like a fable. The mine could not move. The city could. Block by block, Karuna is relocating itself [music] 3 km to the east. Thousands of homes, 6,000 people, a new center already standing around, a new town hall. The old clock tower was carried over and raised again beside it so that not even [music] the hours would be lost. Most buildings are taken down and rebuilt, but 39 of them, the ones [music] holding the town's soul, are being moved home. [music] And on the 19th of August 2025, the greatest [music] of them took its walk. The wooden church of Kiruna, 113 years [music] old, 672 tons, 40 m wide, once voted [music] the most beautiful building in the country, was lifted onto a platform rolling on 224 [music] wheels. Then it was driven at half a kilometer, 5 km across town over 2 days. Thousands of people lined the route in the Arctic summer light. The king of Sweden stood among them and watched a [music] church travel past like a slow red ship. [music] The vicar of Kiruna, Lena Tanberg, gave the blessing as the journey began. And when the wind [music] stole her microphone mid prayer, the crowd's laughter rolled warm down the road. For 9 years, she has said she wished the [music] church good morning and good night through her own kitchen window. She calls the [music] move a day of joy and a day of grief in the same breath. And she does not untangle the two. The mine is why Karuna exists at all, [music] she reminds visitors. Now the ground is cracking and the town does what it has always done. [music] It carries what it loves and keeps living. stand at the new church site [music] in the evening with the mine humming somewhere far below and the northern lights beginning over the rooftops and Sweden's whole [music] quiet character finally comes into focus other countries defend their ground Sweden [music] put its faith in something steadier than ground the patience of its people and their agreement to carry the heavy things together so when [music] the earth itself gave way nobody panicked and nothing was lost. They lifted the city, church and all and set it down where the future could reach it. Lam [music] even now. Not too fast, not too far. Exactly enough. That is Sweden, a country that answers darkness with candles and a cracking earth with patience. If this [music] journey gave you a calm hour tonight, pass it along to someone who could use one and tell us below which moment [music] you would cross the world to stand inside. Subscribing costs nothing and it [music] keeps these long, slow films coming. Somewhere new is already waiting. We will meet you there.
